title: Romanian grammar
intro: A working reference for beginners to intermediate learners. Every pattern comes with real sentences and a translation: read a section, notice the shape, then listen for it in what you watch and read.

sections.title: Nouns, gender & the article on the end
sections.text: Romanian has three genders. **Neuter** nouns behave as masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural: **un tren, două trenuri**. The definite article is glued to the **end** of the noun: **casa** (the house), **orașul** (the city). Feminine nouns in **-ă** swap it for **-a**: casă → casa. After a preposition with no adjective, the article usually drops: **în oraș** (in the city), but **în orașul meu**.

examples.translation: The trains are full in the morning.

sections.title: Genitive & dative (of / to)
sections.text: Nouns change their ending for "of" (genitive) and "to" (dative); the two look the same. When the owned thing has no article right before the owner, Romanian adds **al / a / ai / ale** (agreeing with the thing owned): **o prietenă a mamei**, **un prieten al meu**. The accusative and nominative look the same, so **pe** marks a person as the object: **O văd pe Maria.**

examples.text: Mașina vecinului e în fața casei.
examples.translation: The neighbour's car is in front of the house.
I gave the book to the girl.

examples.text: E un prieten al fratelui meu.
examples.translation: He's a friend of my brother's.

sections.title: Subject pronouns, tu & dumneavoastră
sections.text: The verb ending already shows who is acting, so pronouns are usually dropped: **Vorbesc puțin românește.** The polite **dumneavoastră** (written **dvs.**) takes the voi form of the verb: **Sunteți din București?** A milder polite form, **dumneata**, is used with the tu form.

examples.text: Sunt din Anglia, dar locuiesc la Iași.
examples.translation: I'm from England, but I live in Iași.

sections.title: Present tense (regular verbs)
sections.rule: Many -a verbs add -ez- and many -i verbs add -esc-; learn each verb with its eu form.
sections.text: The present covers habits, facts, what's happening right now and the near future: **Ce faci?** (What are you doing? / How are you?). The infinitive is quoted with **a**: a lucra, to work. Consonants often change before -i: **cânt → cânți, pot → poți, scriu → scrii**.

examples.translation: She reads a lot on the train.

sections.title: Key irregular verbs
sections.text: Also very common: **a da** (dau, dai, dă…), **a lua** (iau, iei, ia…), **a putea** (pot, poți, poate…), **a veni** (vin, vii, vine…), **a ști** (știu, știi, știe…). In speech **este** is usually **e**. Hunger, thirst and cold use **a-i fi** with a dative pronoun: **mi-e foame, mi-e sete, mi-e frig**.

examples.translation: I'm hungry, shall we go and eat?

examples.text: Am doi frați și o soră.
examples.translation: I have two brothers and a sister.
What do you want to do tonight?

sections.title: Negation
sections.text: **nu** goes before the verb and its pronouns. Double negatives are required: **Nu am văzut pe nimeni.** Unlike Italian or Spanish, **nu** stays even when nimeni or nimic comes first: **Nimeni nu știe.** In speech nu often merges: **n-am, n-ai, n-a**.

head: Pattern
Example
rows: Nu mănânc niciodată carne. | I never eat meat.
Nu văd nimic. | I can't see anything.
Nu e nimeni acasă. | There's nobody home.
Nu mai fumează. | He doesn't smoke any more.

sections.title: Adjectives & agreement
sections.text: Adjectives agree with the noun and normally come **after** it: **o casă mare**. Neuter nouns take the masculine form in the singular and the feminine in the plural: **un tren nou, trenuri noi**. When an adjective goes first for emphasis, it takes the article: **frumoasa ta casă**.

sections.title: Perfect compus (what happened)
sections.rule: am / ai / a / am / ați / au + the past participle, which never changes.
sections.text: This is the everyday past for finished events, and every verb uses **a avea**. Participles: **-a → -at** (lucrat), **-ea / -e → -ut** (văzut, făcut, but scris, pus, spus), **-i → -it** (citit), **-î → -ât** (hotărât). Note **a fi → fost**: **am fost** (I was / I've been).

examples.translation: Yesterday I went to the seaside.

sections.title: Imperfect (how things were)
sections.text: The imperfect describes habits, background and what was going on: **Când eram mic, mergeam des la bunici.** It also softens requests: **Voiam să vă întreb ceva** (I wanted to ask you something).

examples.translation: It was raining and it was cold.

examples.text: Pe vremea aceea lucram într-o bancă.
examples.translation: Back then I worked in a bank.

sections.title: Perfect compus vs imperfect
sections.text: Ask: is it a single finished event (perfect compus) or the backdrop to one (imperfect)? Storytelling in writing also uses the **perfect simplu** (cântai, merse), common in literature and in parts of Oltenia, but rare in everyday speech elsewhere.

head: Perfect compus
Imperfect
rows: background, habit, what was going on
the events that move it forward
a sunat telefonul | the phone rang
când dormeam | while I was sleeping

examples.text: Citeam când a sunat cineva la ușă.
examples.translation: I was reading when someone rang the doorbell.

examples.text: În fiecare vară mergeam la mare, dar anul trecut am rămas acasă.
examples.translation: Every summer we went to the seaside, but last year we stayed home.

sections.title: Conjunctiv (să + verb)
sections.rule: să + present form, except the el / ea / ei / ele form, which changes (usually -e ↔ -ă).
sections.text: Where English uses "to + verb", Romanian usually uses **să** + a conjugated verb: **Vreau să plec** (I want to leave), **Trebuie să învăț** (I have to study), **Pot să intru?** (Can I come in?). It also follows wishes and suggestions: **Să mergem!** (Let's go!).

examples.translation: He has to leave at six.

sections.title: The future: voi, o să, am să
sections.text: News and writing use **voi / vei / va … + infinitive**; conversation prefers **o să** (unchanging) + the conjunctiv. **am să / ai să …** is another spoken form. The present also works for plans: **Mâine plec.**

examples.text: Guvernul va anunța noile măsuri mâine.
examples.translation: The government will announce the new measures tomorrow.

sections.title: Object pronouns & the hyphen
sections.text: Pronouns go before the verb and lose a vowel before another vowel, joined with a hyphen: **m-am trezit, l-am văzut, mi-a spus, i-am dat**. With the perfect compus, feminine **o** goes after the participle: **am văzut-o**. Known people as objects are usually doubled: **Îl cunosc pe Andrei. Îi dau Mariei o carte.**

examples.translation: I met him on the street yesterday.

examples.note: a-i plăcea: literally it pleased me

sections.title: Reflexive verbs & se
sections.text: Many everyday verbs are reflexive in Romanian: **a se duce** (to go), **a se uita** (to look), **a-și aminti** (to remember, with a dative pronoun: îmi amintesc). **se** also makes impersonal and passive sentences: **Aici se vorbește engleză. Nu se știe.**

head: Person
a se trezi | to wake up
a se numi | to be called

examples.note: a se vedea: to see each other

examples.text: Cum se spune asta în română?
examples.translation: How do you say this in Romanian?

sections.title: Conditional (would)
sections.text: **aș / ai / ar / am / ați / ar + infinitive** gives "would". Unlike most Romance languages, both halves of an imagined "if" use it: **Dacă aș avea timp, aș călători.** For the past: **Dacă aș fi știut, aș fi venit.** **Aș vrea** is the polite "I'd like".

examples.text: Aș vrea o cafea, vă rog.
Dacă ar ploua, am rămâne acasă.
examples.translation: If it rained, we'd stay home.

examples.text: Ar fi trebuit să plecăm mai devreme.

sections.title: One-page memory map
points: The article sits on the end of the noun: un oraș → orașul, o casă → casa.
Neuter nouns: masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural (un tren, două trenuri).
-ului, -ei, -lor mean of / to the; al, a, ai, ale link an owner after a gap.
pe marks a person as the object, and the pronoun doubles it: îl văd pe Ion.
The verb ending says who's acting, so subject pronouns are usually dropped.
Perfect compus (am făcut) tells what happened; imperfect (făceam) paints the background.
Where English says to + verb, Romanian says să + verb: vreau să plec.
Future: o să merg in speech, voi merge in writing.
Pronouns join the next word with a hyphen: l-am văzut, mi-a spus.
Double negatives are required, and nu stays: nimeni nu știe.
Conditional on both sides of an imagined if: dacă aș avea, aș face.
sections.tip: Listening strategy: the ending of the noun tells you whether it's "a", "the" or "of the" (oraș, orașul, orașului), so listen to the last syllable. ă, â and î are real vowels, not ornaments: fată (a girl) vs fata (the girl), peste (over) vs pește (fish).
